title: Ambapali's garden
hook: the courtesan of Vesali refuses a fortune for the Buddha's meal, gives her mango grove to the order, and later becomes a nun

segments.voice: Yesterday: viriya, the energy of Sona, the mother of ten who began late. Your line: never too late. Today, a garden.

Chariots on the road outside Vesali, going fast. In one of them rides Ambapali, the courtesan of Vesali. She has just heard the Buddha is staying in her own mango grove, so she drove out, sat with him, and asked him to eat at her house tomorrow. He accepted, by staying silent. Now, heading home, she meets the chariots of the Licchavi princes, the ruling families of the town, and drives straight at them, axle to axle, wheel to wheel. What's going on, Ambapali? The Buddha is coming to her house tomorrow, she says. And the princes want that meal for themselves.
screen: `CHARIOTS ON THE ROAD.` → `SHE INVITED HIM FIRST.` → `THE PRINCES WANT THE MEAL.`

segments.voice: First, the offer. In the Great Discourse on the Buddha's final journey, the princes ask her to give up the meal, and offer her a great sum of money. She refuses. Even if you gave me Vesali and all its lands, she says, I wouldn't give up this meal. The princes snap their fingers: we've been beaten by the mango woman! Second, the Buddha. The princes ride on to the grove and invite him themselves. He tells them he has already accepted Ambapali's invitation. Hers came first, so it stands, even against the princes'. Third, the gift. The next day she serves the Buddha and the monks with her own hands. When the meal is done, she sits to one side and gives the mango grove to the community of monks, with the Buddha at its head. He accepts it. Fourth, later. Tradition says Ambapali herself went forth as a nun. Her verses in the Therigatha look back at her own beauty, part by part, her hair, her eyes, her voice, her hands, and how age changed each one. Verse after verse ends with the same refrain: the word of the truth-speaker is not otherwise. A woman who gave away a lovely grove later let go of her own loveliness too, and wrote it down plainly. The mango grove.
screen: `SHE WON'T SELL THE MEAL.` · `HER INVITATION CAME FIRST.` · `SHE GIVES THE GROVE.` · `HER VERSES ON AGE.` · then, large: `THE MANGO GROVE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you own that's actually beautiful, not just something you're finished with: a book you love, a plant, something you made yourself. Ambapali didn't give leftovers; she gave her grove. Imagine handing your beautiful thing to someone who would treasure it, and notice what that feels like, without deciding anything.
Ambapali's garden. The mango grove the courtesan of Vesali gave to the order, after refusing a fortune for the Buddha's meal. Today's word.
Your line: the mango grove. First her grove, and later her beauty: she let both go. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ambapali's meal and gift of her grove are read in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the account of the Buddha's last journey, and her verses on aging in the Therigatha.

original.note: Pali amba means mango; tradition says she was found as a baby at the foot of a mango tree.

chat.says: Did the princes get the Buddha's meal by paying Ambapali more?
options: No: she refused their money, and her invitation, made first, stood.
Yes, the Buddha went wherever the richest offer was made that day.
Yes, the princes outranked her, so the Buddha ate with them.
chat.meaning: In DN 16, Ambapali won't give up the meal even for Vesali, and the Buddha tells the princes he has already accepted her invitation.

Ambapali.meaning: a courtesan of Vesali who gave her mango grove to the monks

Therigatha.meaning: the verses of the elder nuns, in the Pali canon

notes: All paraphrased; Rhys Davids translated DN 16 (1881, 1910), but the writer was not certain of the exact wording.

Confirm DN 16 details: she drove out to the grove; silent acceptance; she drove 'axle to axle, wheel to wheel' against the Licchavis; their offer (a hundred thousand, number omitted); her refusal 'even for Vesali with its lands'; 'beaten by the mango woman'; gift of the grove to the sangha headed by the Buddha.
Her going forth is attributed to tradition (commentary links it to her son Vimala-Kondanna's teaching; omitted).

Therigatha 13.1: confirm the parts of the body she names and the refrain 'the word of the truth-speaker is not otherwise'. Day 755 (Khema's mirror) also touched beauty and aging; this day keeps that to the last section.
Original: name gloss and the mango-tree birth story are attributed to tradition; confirm.
